title: Toyota Bets on Robots That Learn from People
paragraphs: The Japanese carmaker Toyota is betting that robots that learn by watching human workers can help solve a growing problem in Japan: the loss of skilled workers.

On September 18, 2026, Toyota announced plans to introduce 400,000 robots that it has developed itself at about 60 factories around the world, starting in 2028. The company estimates that the project will cost about 1 trillion yen, or roughly $6.4 billion, a year. However, this figure is only an estimate. It also includes both humanoid and non-humanoid machines, as well as replacements for existing equipment, so the number of truly new robots will be much lower.

A key part of the plan is a robot called ELEY, which stands for Embodied Learning Robot for Enhanced Yield. It was developed with the Toyota Research Institute. ELEY does not walk. Instead, it moves on wheels and has two arms with two-fingered hands. Its joints are designed to match the size of an average adult Japanese man, so that human movements can be copied more easily.

Rather than being programmed for every task, ELEY learns by watching people. Workers wear devices shaped like ELEY's hands while they do routine tasks, and the robot observes them through cameras and builds a model of how to do the job. The robot uses an AI method based on the same type of technology behind many AI image generators. In one demonstration in September 2026, ELEY learned to fold T-shirts almost perfectly after 1,500 practice attempts over two weeks.

Toyota hopes the robots can help preserve the skills of its roughly 18,000 "takumi," master craftspeople who have spent decades perfecting techniques such as welding and painting. Many of them are close to retirement, and Japan's shrinking workforce makes it hard to train enough replacements.

However, Toyota admits there are challenges. These include making the robots work reliably during long shifts, ensuring that they place parts in exactly the same position every time and building the data systems needed to train them.
Hiroki Nakajima, an executive vice president at Toyota, said the aim is coexistence with humans, not replacement.
